title: Across 171 mouse brain regions, input wiring but not cell-type mix predicted similar task coding, while cell-type mix was the stronger predictor of similar intrinsic spiking (IBL)
abstract: Question: do input wiring and local cell types set the same aspects of regional physiology? Earlier work found that cell-type mix predicts intrinsic spiking similarity more than wiring, and that axonal input predicts which task variables a region encodes, but it did not test cell types for coding. Data: 171 IBL Brain-Wide Map regions with published decoding scores of 5 task variables (coding) and 8 spike features of 62,049 units (intrinsic); Knox 2019 connectome; Allen MERFISH subclass composition. Method: a plan frozen before analysis. For region pairs, phenotype similarity was regressed jointly on input-fingerprint similarity (F_in), output similarity and composition similarity (T), with geometry and sampling controls. The wiring share s is the unique R2 of F_in over the unique R2 of F_in plus T. Inference used 1,000 spatial surrogate maps per family and a leave-one-region-out jackknife. Results: F_in predicted coding similarity beyond T (beta 0.17, surrogate p = 0.011), but T did not (beta -0.02, p = 0.66). The wiring share was 0.98 for coding and 0.25 for intrinsic phenotype (difference 0.73, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.14; Holm p = 0.0004). The F_in beta was equal in the two families; the T beta was lower for coding (difference -0.26, CI -0.41 to -0.12). Independent Steinmetz 2019 coding data gave the same direction (F_in 0.16, p = 0.045; T -0.05) with a wide interval. An inheritance model agreed: coding followed input sources, not similar-cell-mix regions. Limitations: correlational, region-level, one connectome and one MERFISH brain; small unique variances make the ratio noisy; the coding link depends mostly on feedback decoding and partly on the thalamus; coding reliability could not be measured.
